title: Nebulous, but no nebula
caption: The globular cluster Messier 28, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 28 · constellation Sagittarius · about 18000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, J. E. Grindlay et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: In bright, sharp detail, Hubble reveals Messier 28, a globular cluster lying in Sagittarius, the Archer. It lies about 18 000 light-years from Earth.

When Charles Messier added it to his list in 1764, he described it as a '[round] nebula containing no star'. That was not as strange as it sounds. Until the early twentieth century, 'nebula' meant any hazy, poorly defined light in the sky, and all 110 objects Messier identified were gathered under the title Catalog of Nebulae and Star Clusters. Star clusters and even supernova remnants were lumped together as nebulae.

Messier's mistake is understandable. From Earth, even through binoculars, the cluster appears only as a very faint smudge, because the atmosphere's distorting effects blur it, and larger telescopes are needed to pick out single stars. From space, Hubble shows it clearly as the star cluster it really is.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.71 x 2.64 arcminutes) and distance (18000 light years), the frame spans roughly 14 × 14 light-years. Its light set out about 18,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from violet light through visible and hydrogen-alpha to the near-infrared. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through binoculars Messier 28 is only a very faint smudge, but from above the atmosphere Hubble resolves its individual stars.

explore: Today, a nebula means a vast, often glowing cloud of interstellar dust and ionized gas. This image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 across a range of visible and near-infrared filters, including one that isolates glowing hydrogen.
alt: A globular cluster shown in sharp detail, with many individual stars.
